newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian opposition unites to oust Iliescu.
newsitem.headline: Romanian opposition unites to oust Iliescu.

text.p: Romania's two main opposition groups joined forces on Thursday in a bid to oust incumbent Ion Iliescu in presidential elections and complete the rout of former Communists after their defeat in parliamentary polls.

The pact pledges support to Emil Constantinescu, who ran second in the opening round of the presidential poll to Iliescu, Romania's leader since 1989. The two men will clash head-on in a run-off on November 17.
Constantinescu and ex-prime minister Petre Roman, third in the presidential contest, signed the agreement in a former royal palace, embraced and waved victory signs.
"On November 3 Romania took one giant step towards a new era -- but this step is not complete," Constantinescu said, referring to the centrist opposition's parliamentary election win.

"It is vital that victory on November 17 should belong to democratic forces too. Only then will things straighten out. We have a parliamentary majority and the government will be formed within a few days."
Final results in the first round of the presidential poll, released on Thursday, gave Iliescu 32 percent of the vote. Constantinescu had 28 percent and Roman 21 percent.
Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) led the parliament vote with 30 percent, to 23 for Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PSDR). Roman's Social Democrats were third.
The new alliance heralded an era of "truly democratic government", said Constantinescu, a professor who had no political career under Communism.
He said the pact's signature was doubly historic because it coincided with the 79th anniversary of Russia's Bolshevik revolution.
"For us, November 7 will mark a historic moment -- another kind of history than that marking the birth of Communism, which made generations suffer in humiliation," he said.
The opposition says Romania cannot emerge from the shadow of Communism until it rids itself of Iliescu, a politician under executed dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Iliescu has conceded that his party will now go into parliamentary opposition but urges voters to re-elect him as president to preserve stability and soften the social impact of reform.
"Constantinescu's programme means turning back the clock of history not to 1989 but to the 1930s when the rich were in control," he told a rally in the southern town of Slobozia.
Iliescu claims there is no certainty Roman's first-round voters will switch their backing to Constantinescu.

Roman was Iliescu's prime minister for 22 months, before being ousted in 1991 by anti-reform riots staged by miners. He said the pact had been concluded in less than two hours and dismissed suggestions of a rift among its members.

Although the accord's main aim is to win the elections, it also set down a power-sharing formula. Constantinescu's CDR is due to get the prime minister's job, with a deputy prime minister and the head of the upper house, the Senate, going to Roman's USD.
The new government and its programme would be announced when parliament sits on November 23, Constantinescu said.
Under the pact, the new government's policies will blend elements from the campaign manifestos of both parties, including tax cuts, currency liberalisation and steps to curb inflation.

Analysts say the new government will have to abandon some costly promises to win the confidence of Western financial institutions. The International Monetary Fund suspended credits this year after criticising aspects of economic policy.
